disease_info: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, either directly, as a witness, or through learning about it happening to close others. It is characterized by intrusive re-experiencing of the trauma, avoidance of reminders, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and marked changes in arousal and reactivity lasting longer than one month and causing significant functional impairment. The clinical course may be acute or chronic, with onset soon after the trauma or delayed by months; it often fluctuates with triggers such as anniversaries or situational reminders. PTSD is distinguished from depression and generalized anxiety disorders by the requirement for a qualifying traumatic event and the presence of specific re-experiencing and avoidance phenomena anchored to that event.

narrative.personality: Dana is a structured, community-oriented organizer who enjoys bringing people together through church, neighborhood events, and volunteer work while taking pride in careful planning and budgeting.
narrative.stressor: About two and a half years ago, Dana separated from her husband after a long period of escalating emotional volatility that culminated in a single terrifying night when he became physically violent during an argument about money, trapping her in their apartment, smashing objects, and threatening to kill her before neighbors called the police. Before that night, she saw herself as someone who could defuse conflict and hold a household together with structure and faith, and she initially tried to frame the incident as a one-time loss of control, throwing herself into church activities and community planning to avoid fully processing what had happened. Over the following months, however, her sense of safety eroded: she left her job because she could not concentrate or tolerate being around certain people, moved into a small apartment alone, and gradually withdrew from many of the social roles that had defined her, leading to mounting financial strain and feelings of failure about her stalled project-management plans. After more than two years of living with this ongoing disruption—finding it harder to attend church, cook, or garden without being abruptly pulled back to that night—she finally sought psychiatric help when her pastor and a close friend urged her to talk to someone, and she recognized that her daily life was being dominated by unwanted recollections she could not control.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep getting these memories of what happened with my husband that pop into my head out of nowhere, and I can’t shut them off.”

narrative.personality: Austin is a meticulous, checklist-driven problem solver who enjoys teaching others and being the outgoing, dependable guy at work and in his community sports and volunteer circles.
narrative.stressor: Just over two years ago, during an overnight maintenance shift at the plant, Austin was involved in a serious industrial accident when a press malfunctioned while he and a younger coworker were troubleshooting a jam; despite his safety talk earlier that evening, a guard was bypassed, and the machine crushed the coworker’s arm so badly it had to be amputated. As the senior mechanic on duty, he coordinated the emergency response and later had to walk investigators step-by-step through the sequence of events, replaying his decisions and feeling increasingly convinced he had personally failed the man he had been mentoring. In the months that followed, he stayed on the job but found that the plant, which had always been his source of pride and camaraderie, now felt like a place of constant tension and self-doubt, and he began overcompensating with extra checks, long hours, and avoidance of certain tasks while his usual enjoyment of softball, barbecues, and community workshops diminished. After two years of living with a pervasive sense of guilt and a dark, joyless mood that his friends at the senior center started to notice, he agreed to see a psychiatrist when his supervisor gently suggested that the incident still seemed to be “eating him up inside” and was affecting how he carried himself at work and with the crew.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since that accident at the plant, I’ve just felt this constant weight of guilt and anger I can’t shake, like a dark cloud that never really lifts.”

narrative.personality: Damon is a disciplined, intellectually curious retired historian who enjoys orderly projects, mentoring youth, and quiet hobbies like woodworking, gardening, and classical music.
narrative.stressor: A little over two years ago, Damon was driving home from a local theater performance with his wife when a speeding truck ran a red light and struck their car broadside, sending it spinning into a ditch; he remained conscious throughout the crash and its aftermath, trapped in the vehicle while his wife was unconscious beside him and emergency crews worked to cut them out. Although both ultimately survived, he spent days in the hospital watching his wife in the ICU and was repeatedly told by physicians and relatives how close they had come to dying, reinforcing his awareness of the life-threatening nature of the event. Before the accident, he had led a calm, well-structured retirement built around archival projects, gardening, and birdwatching, but in the months after, he found himself unable to relax in his own home, subtly reorganizing his environment, double- and triple-checking locks and windows, and giving up many of his solitary walks and photography outings because he no longer felt safe in open or unfamiliar spaces. After more than two years of this constant on-edge existence—straining his enjoyment of time with his wife, disrupting his mentoring commitments, and leaving him exhausted—he agreed to see a psychiatrist at his primary care doctor’s urging, recognizing that his persistent need to be on guard had grown far beyond what could be explained by normal caution after an accident.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since the car accident, I feel like I can never really let my guard down—I’m always scanning everything around me, even at home.”
